### R3-01 · Quick review

Syntax of a multi-row INSERT, and its two advantages?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

`INSERT INTO t (a, b) VALUES (1, 2), (3, 4);`. It is more convenient and usually faster than many single INSERTs, and it is all-or-nothing if a row breaks a constraint.
</details>

### R3-02 · Predict the output

Dataset `mfa`:

```sql
INSERT INTO "collections" ("title", "accession_number") VALUES ('A', 'x1'), ('B', '56.257');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM "collections";
```
What is printed?

A. `4`
B. `5`
C. `6`
D. `ERROR: UNIQUE constraint failed`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**D**. The second row duplicates an accession number. The statement fails, and neither row is inserted.
</details>

### R3-03 · Quick review

Two ways to import a CSV with `.import`, and when to use each?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

`.import --csv --skip 1 file.csv existing_table` when the columns match the table. `.import --csv file.csv new_table` (the header names the columns), then `INSERT INTO real (...) SELECT ... FROM new_table;` and `DROP TABLE new_table;` when they don't (e.g. no id column).
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture3 L604-605](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“one to import into an existing table and one to import into a brand new table”*</sub>

### R3-05 · Predict the output

Dataset `mfa`:

```sql
DELETE FROM "collections" WHERE "acquired" < '1912-01-01';
SELECT "title" FROM "collections" ORDER BY "id";
```
What is printed?

A. `Profusion of Flowers; Spring Outing`
B. `Imaginative Landscape; Profusion of Flowers; Spring Outing`
C. `Spring Outing`
D. `(no rows)`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. Farmers (1911) is deleted. `NULL < date` is not true, so Imaginative Landscape stays.
</details>

### R3-06 · Concept check

Which ON DELETE action turns "delete the artist, then their links" into one step?

A. RESTRICT
B. NO ACTION
C. SET NULL
D. CASCADE

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**D**. CASCADE deletes the referencing rows automatically. SET NULL would keep them with artist_id = NULL.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture3 L1010-1013](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“Or perhaps, most compellingly, I could try to CASCADE the deletion.”*</sub>

### R3-07 · Predict the output

Dataset `votes`:

```sql
UPDATE "votes" SET "title" = upper(trim("title"));
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT "title") FROM "votes";
```
What is printed?

A. `4`
B. `9`
C. `12`
D. `20`

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. trim and upper merge the whitespace and case variants, but the typos remain as their own groups: FAMERS…, FARMESR…, FARMERS WORKING, IMAGINTIVE…, and PROFUSION. That gives 4 + 5 = 9.

</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture3 L1330-1339](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“But there's still some typos”*</sub>

### R3-08 · Concept check

In a `BEFORE DELETE` trigger, how do you refer to the title of the row being deleted?

A. NEW.title
B. OLD.title
C. DELETED.title
D. title

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**B**. OLD is the row being removed. NEW exists only for INSERT and UPDATE.
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture3 L1604-1608](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“So old.title gives me access to the old row”*</sub>

### R3-10 · Quick review

What is a soft delete, and one ethical concern?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Marking a row as deleted (e.g. deleted = 1) instead of removing it. For personal data it may not honour a user's request to be forgotten (GDPR).
</details>

<sub>Source: [lecture3 L1774-1784](../sources/lecture3.txt) *“and the right to be forgotten”*</sub>
